meta.title: Who really said "Hugo sent his publisher a telegram reading ? and the publisher replied !"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Hugo's ? telegram and his publisher's ! reply is almost certainly fiction. The joke ran without Hugo in 1850 and was first told of him in an 1892 book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hugo sent his publisher a telegram reading ? and the publisher replied !'?
meta.ogDescription: The famous ? / ! exchange between Victor Hugo and his publisher is almost certainly a recycled 1850 newspaper joke, first pinned on Hugo in 1892.

answer.label: Not Victor Hugo — an older anonymous joke
answer.authorDates: Unsigned newspaper joke, earliest known 1850; first told of Hugo in 1892
answer.sourceLine: No letter or telegram from Hugo has ever been produced. Quote Investigator ↗ traces a one-character exchange to an anonymous English newspaper item of 1850 with no Hugo in it. The earliest Hugo version it found is William S. Walsh’s Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (1892), where the message is a letter, not a telegram. QI judges the story most likely fictional.

source.excerpt: But the shortest correspondence ever known took place between Victor Hugo and his publisher, just after the publication of “Les Miserables.” The poet, impatient to learn of the success of the book, sent off a letter which contained only the following: ? and he received the following entirely satisfactory answer: !
source.trailTitle: How the joke attached itself to Hugo
trail: 1850: An anonymous item in the Nottinghamshire Guardian (25 April) describes a one-character letter, a question mark, answered with a cipher meaning there was no news. Hugo is not in it. Reprinted widely in Britain and the US, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1892: William S. Walsh’s Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (p. 600) is the earliest Hugo version QI found. Hugo sends his unnamed publisher a letter containing only “?”. Internet Archive scan ↗

1981: The Guinness Book of World Records (p. 216) names the publisher as Hurst and Blackett and dates the exchange to 1862. Wikipedia’s Hugo article cites it and calls the whole story “an apocryphal tale” ↗.
2006: A Times column by Ben Macintyre (4 March) tells it as a telegram. This is the only source Wikiquote ↗ gives for listing “?” among Hugo’s quotes.
source.excerptNote: An anthology of anecdotes compiled thirty years after the novel appeared, with no source given. Quote Investigator notes that it closely matches an anonymous newspaper joke from 1850.

sourceLink.text: Walsh, Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities: full text at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The popular “telegram” wording is an anonymous modern retelling with no single identifiable source, so no copyright status is claimed for it. The 1892 Walsh passage shown in the excerpt is a US publication from before 1931, so it is in the public domain.

author.name: Victor Hugo
author.kicker: The man the story is told about
author.heading: About Victor Hugo
author.bio: Victor Hugo (1802–1885) was the towering figure of French Romanticism. He wrote Les Misérables (1862), the novel whose success the “?” / “!” story is meant to celebrate. He spent many years in political exile, fifteen of them on the Channel island of Guernsey. He is a constant magnet for invented quotes and anecdotes, and this one is among the best known.

misattribution.heading: What the popular version gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The story is told with confident details: Hugo, a telegram, a named publisher, 1862. None of them is supported by a primary record.

items.why: No such letter or telegram survives. The Hugo version first appears in 1892, in a book of anecdotes that gives no source. Quote Investigator ↗ calls it implausibly late, says it resembles the 1850 joke, and judges these tales most likely fictional.
The earliest Hugo version, Walsh’s Handy-Book, says Hugo “sent off a letter.” Full text ↗

This name comes from the 1981 Guinness Book of World Records. Hurst and Blackett were the London publishers of Lascelles Wraxall’s English translation (October 1862). The original French edition was published by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven & Cie ↗.
A 2013 business book retells the “?” telegram and “!” reply about Wilde. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive support for it either.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest version Quote Investigator ↗ found is an anonymous English newspaper joke from 1850 that does not mention Hugo. It was first told of Hugo in 1892 and is most likely fiction.

context.heading: Why the story survives
lead: The story is a perfect anecdote: an anxious author, a triumphant reply, and two punctuation marks. That is why it keeps getting reprinted as “the shortest correspondence in history.” Over time it collected details such as a holiday, a telegram, a named London firm and an exact year. Those details make it sound documented when it is not.

The pattern, a one-character question and a one-character answer, was already circulating as an anonymous joke in English newspapers in 1850. According to Quote Investigator ↗, it attached itself to Hugo only in an 1892 anthology, and later to Oscar Wilde.
context.detailsSummary: Why Wikiquote lists it as a Hugo quote
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s Victor Hugo page ↗ includes “?” in its main quotes list. Its only source is Ben Macintyre’s 4 March 2006 column in The Times, a modern retelling and not a primary record. Quote Investigator’s dated search of earlier printed sources is the stronger evidence, and English Wikipedia’s Hugo article follows it in calling the tale apocryphal.

Walsh, Handy-book of literary curiosities, Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott Co.; item dated 1893 with a stated copyright date of 1892
Wikiquote lists '?' in Hugo's main Quotes section as a telegram to his publisher about Les Misérables, sourced to Ben Macintyre, The Times, 4 March 2006

Wikipedia calls it 'An apocryphal tale' about Hugo and his publisher Hurst and Blackett in 1862, citing Quote Investigator and Guinness Book of World Records 1981 p. 216; gives Hugo's dates 1802–1885 and his 15 years of exile on Guernsey
Les Misérables was published by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven & Cie.; Lascelles Wraxall's first British translation was published in London by Hurst and Blackett, October 1862
